claim: Damaging GATA6 variants cause cardiac outflow tract defects, sometimes with pancreatic and diaphragmic malformations.
source: Damaging GATA6 variants cause cardiac outflow tract defects, sometimes with pancreatic and diaphragmic malformations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of known clinical associations with GATA6 variants.

claim: GATA6 is a pioneer factor in cardiac development.
source: We show that GATA6 is a pioneer factor in cardiac development, regulating SMYD1 that activates HAND2, and KDR that with HAND2 orchestrates outflow tract formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data showing GATA6 binding to closed chromatin and subsequent gene activation.

claim: GATA6 regulates SMYD1 that activates HAND2.
source: We show that GATA6 is a pioneer factor in cardiac development, regulating SMYD1 that activates HAND2, and KDR that with HAND2 orchestrates outflow tract formation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing reduced SMYD1 and HAND2 expression in GATA6 mutant cells.

claim: KDR with HAND2 orchestrates outflow tract formation.
source: We show that GATA6 is a pioneer factor in cardiac development, regulating SMYD1 that activates HAND2, and KDR that with HAND2 orchestrates outflow tract formation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing reduced KDR expression in GATA6 mutant cells and known roles of these genes in outflow tract development.

claim: GATA6 LoF variants perturbed cardiac genes and endoderm lineage genes that direct PDX1 expression and pancreatic development.
source: LoF variants perturbed cardiac genes and also endoderm lineage genes that direct PDX1 expression and pancreatic development.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing altered expression of cardiac and endodermal genes in GATA6 LoF mutant cells.

claim: An exon 4 GATA6 missense variant is highly associated with extra-cardiac malformations.
source: Remarkably, an exon 4 GATA6 missense variant, highly associated with extra-cardiac malformations, caused ectopic pioneer activities, profoundly diminishing GATA4, FOXA1/2, and PDX1 expression and increasing normal retinoic acid signaling that promotes diaphragm development.
evidence: This is supported by clinical data showing that 9 of 11 patients with exon 4 missense variants had pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

claim: The exon 4 GATA6 missense variant caused ectopic pioneer activities.
source: Remarkably, an exon 4 GATA6 missense variant, highly associated with extra-cardiac malformations, caused ectopic pioneer activities, profoundly diminishing GATA4, FOXA1/2, and PDX1 expression and increasing normal retinoic acid signaling that promotes diaphragm development.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing ~44,000 augmented and ectopic peaks in GATA6R456G/R456G cells.

claim: The exon 4 GATA6 missense variant profoundly diminished GATA4, FOXA1/2, and PDX1 expression.
source: Remarkably, an exon 4 GATA6 missense variant, highly associated with extra-cardiac malformations, caused ectopic pioneer activities, profoundly diminishing GATA4, FOXA1/2, and PDX1 expression and increasing normal retinoic acid signaling that promotes diaphragm development.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing markedly reduced expression of these genes in GATA6R456G/R456G cells.

claim: The exon 4 GATA6 missense variant increased retinoic acid signaling that promotes diaphragm development.
source: Remarkably, an exon 4 GATA6 missense variant, highly associated with extra-cardiac malformations, caused ectopic pioneer activities, profoundly diminishing GATA4, FOXA1/2, and PDX1 expression and increasing normal retinoic acid signaling that promotes diaphragm development.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased expression of RA signaling genes (ALDH1A2, RARA, RARB, STRA6, HOXB1) in GATA6R456G/R456G cells.

claim: Congenital heart disease occurs in approximately 1% of newborns.
source: Congenital heart disease (CHD), the leading birth defect worldwide that occurs in approximately 1% of newborns (van der Linde et al., 2011), comprises a range of structural malformations arising during embryonic development (Zaidi and Brueckner, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van der Linde et al., 2011.

claim: CHD is the leading birth defect worldwide.
source: Congenital heart disease (CHD), the leading birth defect worldwide that occurs in approximately 1% of newborns (van der Linde et al., 2011), comprises a range of structural malformations arising during embryonic development (Zaidi and Brueckner, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Contemporary treatments for CHD enable survival into adulthood.
source: Contemporary treatments for CHD enables survival into adulthood, but many patients have ongoing medical problems related to extra-cardiac malformations and/or neurodevelopmental disabilities (Brickner et al., 2000; Marino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brickner et al., 2000 and Marino et al., 2012.

claim: Many CHD patients have ongoing medical problems related to extra-cardiac malformations and/or neurodevelopmental disabilities.
source: Contemporary treatments for CHD enables survival into adulthood, but many patients have ongoing medical problems related to extra-cardiac malformations and/or neurodevelopmental disabilities (Brickner et al., 2000; Marino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brickner et al., 2000 and Marino et al., 2012.

claim: The first heart field creates the left ventricle and portions of the atria.
source: Early in cardiogenesis, the first heart field creates the left ventricle and portions of the atria, while the second heart field gives rise to the right ventricle and outflow tract, with contributions from neural crest cells (Buckingham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buckingham et al., 2005.

claim: The second heart field gives rise to the right ventricle and outflow tract, with contributions from neural crest cells.
source: Early in cardiogenesis, the first heart field creates the left ventricle and portions of the atria, while the second heart field gives rise to the right ventricle and outflow tract, with contributions from neural crest cells (Buckingham et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buckingham et al., 2005.

claim: Dominant human loss of function variants in TBX5, NKX2-5, and GATA4 cause atrial and ventricular septal defects.
source: For example, dominant human loss of function (LoF) variants in TBX5, NKX2-5, and GATA4 that are highly expressed in the first and second heart fields cause atrial and ventricular septal defects (Basson et al., 1997; Benson et al., 1999; Garg et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basson et al., 1997; Benson et al., 1999; Garg et al., 2003.

claim: GATA6 is expressed in the first heart field.
source: GATA6, while expressed in the first heart field (Morrisey et al., 1996), plays particularly critical roles in the developing second heart field (Molkentin, 2000) and in recruitment of cardiac neural crest lineages (Lepore et al., 2006) that together shape the cardiac outflow tract.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morrisey et al., 1996.

claim: GATA6 plays particularly critical roles in the developing second heart field.
source: GATA6, while expressed in the first heart field (Morrisey et al., 1996), plays particularly critical roles in the developing second heart field (Molkentin, 2000) and in recruitment of cardiac neural crest lineages (Lepore et al., 2006) that together shape the cardiac outflow tract.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Molkentin, 2000.

claim: GATA6 plays a role in recruitment of cardiac neural crest lineages that shape the cardiac outflow tract.
source: GATA6, while expressed in the first heart field (Morrisey et al., 1996), plays particularly critical roles in the developing second heart field (Molkentin, 2000) and in recruitment of cardiac neural crest lineages (Lepore et al., 2006) that together shape the cardiac outflow tract.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lepore et al., 2006.

claim: CHD patients with GATA6 mutations have a striking preponderance of outflow tract malformations.
source: Consistent with these developmental functions, CHD patients with GATA6 mutations have a striking preponderance of outflow tract malformations (Gharibeh et al., 2018; Kodo et al., 2009; Maitra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gharibeh et al., 2018; Kodo et al., 2009; Maitra et al., 2010.

claim: GATA6 is critical for endodermal development.
source: GATA6 also is critical for endodermal development (Fisher et al., 2017), and some CHD patients with damaging GATA6 variants also have pancreatic agenesis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Yu et al., 2014) or other abdominal malformations (Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fisher et al., 2017.

claim: Some CHD patients with damaging GATA6 variants have pancreatic agenesis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia or other abdominal malformations.
source: GATA6 also is critical for endodermal development (Fisher et al., 2017), and some CHD patients with damaging GATA6 variants also have pancreatic agenesis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Yu et al., 2014) or other abdominal malformations (Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2014; Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017.

claim: Physical interactions of NKX2-5, TBX5, and GATA4 proteins modulate the expression of other cardiac genes.
source: Developmental transcription factors work in concert to exert network-level effects on organogenesis (Luna-Zurita et al., 2016): physical interactions of NKX2-5, TBX5, and GATA4 proteins modulate the expression of other cardiac genes (Garg et al., 2003; Hiroi et al., 2001; Bruneau et al., 2001; Maitra et al., 2009) while GATA6 and GATA4 proteins together promote pancreatic development (Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garg et al., 2003; Hiroi et al., 2001; Bruneau et al., 2001; Maitra et al., 2009.

claim: GATA6 and GATA4 proteins together promote pancreatic development.
source: Developmental transcription factors work in concert to exert network-level effects on organogenesis (Luna-Zurita et al., 2016): physical interactions of NKX2-5, TBX5, and GATA4 proteins modulate the expression of other cardiac genes (Garg et al., 2003; Hiroi et al., 2001; Bruneau et al., 2001; Maitra et al., 2009) while GATA6 and GATA4 proteins together promote pancreatic development (Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017.

claim: Members of the GATA family of transcription factors serve as endodermal pioneer factors.
source: Notably, members of the GATA family of transcription factors serve as endodermal pioneer factors that participate with FOXA, also a pioneer factor, to engage and open chromatin and recruit additional transcriptional activators (Fisher et al., 2017; Zaret and Carroll, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 2017; Zaret and Carroll, 2011.

claim: GATA family members participate with FOXA to engage and open chromatin and recruit additional transcriptional activators.
source: Notably, members of the GATA family of transcription factors serve as endodermal pioneer factors that participate with FOXA, also a pioneer factor, to engage and open chromatin and recruit additional transcriptional activators (Fisher et al., 2017; Zaret and Carroll, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 2017; Zaret and Carroll, 2011.

claim: Mice with one inactivated Gata6 allele have either subtle dysmorphic aortic valves or no CHD.
source: While often informative, prior studies of mice with one inactivated Gata6 allele have either subtle dysmorphic aortic valves (Gharibeh et al., 2018) or no CHD (Lepore et al., 2006) and notably lack pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia that occur in human CHD patients with damaging GATA6 variants (Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gharibeh et al., 2018 and Lepore et al., 2006.

claim: Mice with one inactivated Gata6 allele lack pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia that occur in human CHD patients with damaging GATA6 variants.
source: While often informative, prior studies of mice with one inactivated Gata6 allele have either subtle dysmorphic aortic valves (Gharibeh et al., 2018) or no CHD (Lepore et al., 2006) and notably lack pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia that occur in human CHD patients with damaging GATA6 variants (Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gharibeh et al., 2018; Lepore et al., 2006; Chao et al., 2015; De Franco et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2017.

claim: Mice with biallelic Gata6 inactivation have deficits in early visceral endoderm formation resulting in nonviable embryos.
source: Mice with biallelic Gata6 inactivation have deficits in early visceral endoderm formation resulting in nonviable embryos (Morrisey et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2005), which may explain the absence of homozygous GATA6 null alleles in humans, but provide limited insights into organ morphogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morrisey et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2005.

claim: The absence of homozygous GATA6 null alleles in humans may be explained by early embryonic lethality observed in mice with biallelic Gata6 inactivation.
source: Mice with biallelic Gata6 inactivation have deficits in early visceral endoderm formation resulting in nonviable embryos (Morrisey et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2005), which may explain the absence of homozygous GATA6 null alleles in humans, but provide limited insights into organ morphogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on mouse data and the absence of human homozygous null alleles.

claim: Differentiation of hiPSC-CMs activates transcriptional networks that regulate early in vivo human cardiogenesis.
source: The introduction of human CHD mutations using CRISPR/Cas9 (De Franco et al., 2013) into isogenic human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) provides an alternative model system suited for analyzing developmental consequences, as differentiation of these cells activate transcriptional networks that regulate early in vivo human cardiogenesis (DeLaughter et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to DeLaughter et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016.

claim: Nine heterozygous de novo GATA6 variants were identified among >4000 CHD patients studied by WES through the PCGC.
source: Among >4000 CHD patients enrolled and studied by WES through National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute's Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium (PCGC) (Homsy et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2017), we identified nine heterozygous de novo variants: four LoF (LoF) and five damaging missense variants in GATA6 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by WES data from the PCGC cohort and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Four of the nine GATA6 variants identified in PCGC CHD patients were loss of function variants.
source: Among >4000 CHD patients enrolled and studied by WES through National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute's Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium (PCGC) (Homsy et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2017), we identified nine heterozygous de novo variants: four LoF (LoF) and five damaging missense variants in GATA6 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by WES data from the PCGC cohort and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Five of the nine GATA6 variants identified in PCGC CHD patients were damaging missense variants.
source: Among >4000 CHD patients enrolled and studied by WES through National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute's Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium (PCGC) (Homsy et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2017), we identified nine heterozygous de novo variants: four LoF (LoF) and five damaging missense variants in GATA6 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by WES data from the PCGC cohort and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Among 70 damaging GATA6 variants, all caused CHD.
source: We considered whether the distribution of these 70 damaging GATA6 variants (61 published, 9 PCGC) across the 595 encoded GATA6 amino acids correlated with clinical phenotypes (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1A, B). All variants (43 missense, 27 LoF, including eight recurrent variants) caused CHD.
evidence: This is based on clinical data from 70 patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Extra-cardiac phenotypes occurred in 29/70 (41%) patients with GATA6 variants.
source: Extra-cardiac phenotypes occurred in 29/70 (41%) patients, and more often with LoF (18/27) than missense (11/43) variants (p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on clinical data from 70 patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Extra-cardiac phenotypes occurred more often with LoF (18/27) than missense (11/43) GATA6 variants (p<0.001).
source: Extra-cardiac phenotypes occurred in 29/70 (41%) patients, and more often with LoF (18/27) than missense (11/43) variants (p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of clinical data from 70 patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Neurocognitive dysfunction occurred in 13 patients (18.5%) with GATA6 variants.
source: Neurocognitive dysfunction occurred in 13 patients (18.5%).
evidence: This is based on clinical data from 70 patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Pancreatic agenesis/hypoplasia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurred in 20/70 patients (28.5%) with GATA6 variants.
source: Pancreatic agenesis/hypoplasia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurred in 20/70 patients (28.5%) and more frequently with GATA6 LoF (14/27) than missense (9/43) variants (p=0.001).
evidence: This is based on clinical data from 70 patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Pancreatic agenesis/hypoplasia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurred more frequently with GATA6 LoF (14/27) than missense (9/43) variants (p=0.001).
source: Pancreatic agenesis/hypoplasia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurred in 20/70 patients (28.5%) and more frequently with GATA6 LoF (14/27) than missense (9/43) variants (p=0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of clinical data from 70 patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Eleven of 43 GATA6 missense variants altered residues in the DNA-binding zinc finger domain encoded by exon 4.
source: Among 43 GATA6 missense variants, 11 variants altered residues in the DNA-binding zinc finger (ZF) domain encoded by exon 4 (amino acids 435–477), significantly more than expected by chance (p=0.0004).
evidence: This is based on analysis of variant distribution and statistical testing.

claim: The clustering of 11 missense variants in exon 4 is significantly more than expected by chance (p=0.0004).
source: Among 43 GATA6 missense variants, 11 variants altered residues in the DNA-binding zinc finger (ZF) domain encoded by exon 4 (amino acids 435–477), significantly more than expected by chance (p=0.0004).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of variant distribution.

claim: Nine of 11 patients with exon 4 missense variants had pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
source: Nine of these 11 patients with exon four missense variants had pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia, but none of 32 patients with missense variants located elsewhere (p=1.1e-6).
evidence: This is based on clinical data from patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: None of 32 patients with missense variants outside exon 4 had pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia (p=1.1e-6).
source: Nine of these 11 patients with exon four missense variants had pancreatic agenesis or congenital diaphragmatic hernia, but none of 32 patients with missense variants located elsewhere (p=1.1e-6).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of clinical data from patients with GATA6 variants.

claim: Computational modeling positioned residue 456 alongside a polar residue (asparagine 466) in close proximity to DNA.
source: Computational modeling of this domain (PyMOL software) positioned residue 456 alongside a polar residue (asparagine 466) in close proximity to DNA (Bates et al., 2008; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using PyMOL software and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Substitution of a non-polar glycine at residue 456 (R456G) is predicted to disrupt interactions with DNA.
source: Substitution of a non-polar glycine at residue 456 (R456G) is predicted to disrupt these interactions, and potentially alter GATA6 binding to DNA.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and structural predictions.

claim: GATA6+/- hiPSCs exhibited mono-allelic GATA6 expression, suggesting nonsense-mediated decay of RNAs transcribed from targeted alleles.
source: GATA6+/- hiPSCs, unlike WT hiPSCs, exhibited mono-allelic GATA6 expression, suggesting nonsense-mediated decay of RNAs transcribed from targeted alleles.
evidence: This is based on RNA expression data from GATA6+/- hiPSCs.

claim: GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs had weaker fluorescent signal than WT cells.
source: GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs had weaker fluorescent signal than WT cells, while GATA6-/- lines expressed no fluorescence at baseline or during the differentiation protocol (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: GATA6-/- lines expressed no fluorescence at baseline or during the differentiation protocol.
source: GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs had weaker fluorescent signal than WT cells, while GATA6-/- lines expressed no fluorescence at baseline or during the differentiation protocol (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Fewer independent differentiation rounds of GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs contained beating sarcomeres compared to WT.
source: Consistent with these data, at differentiation day eight when contracting sarcomeres were present in WT cells, fewer independent differentiation rounds of GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs contained beating sarcomeres and no GATA6-/- cells showed sarcomeres or spontaneous beating (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on observation of beating cells across multiple differentiation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No GATA6-/- cells showed sarcomeres or spontaneous beating.
source: Consistent with these data, at differentiation day eight when contracting sarcomeres were present in WT cells, fewer independent differentiation rounds of GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs contained beating sarcomeres and no GATA6-/- cells showed sarcomeres or spontaneous beating (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on observation of beating cells across multiple differentiation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GATA6R456G/R456G hiPSC-CMs showed a fluorescence signal comparable to that of GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs.
source: Analogous studies of GATA6R456G/R456G hiPSC-CMs (Figure 2D–F) showed a fluorescence signal comparable to that of GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs and spontaneous beating cells in approximately ~60% of differentiation rounds.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: GATA6R456G/R456G hiPSC-CMs showed spontaneous beating cells in approximately ~60% of differentiation rounds.
source: Analogous studies of GATA6R456G/R456G hiPSC-CMs (Figure 2D–F) showed a fluorescence signal comparable to that of GATA6+/- hiPSC-CMs and spontaneous beating cells in approximately ~60% of differentiation rounds.
evidence: This is based on observation of beating cells across multiple differentiation experiments shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Day 4 WT cells showed expression of both pluripotent stem cell markers and transcriptional modulators associated with early cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: At day 4 of differentiation, RNA-Seq of WT cells showed expression of both pluripotent stem cell markers (e.g., POU5F1 encoding OCT4) and transcriptional modulators associated with early cardiomyocyte differentiation (Figures 3B,C and 4A,B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figures 3B,C and 4A,B.

claim: Day 4 WT primordial cardiomyocytes expressed SMYD1, TBX5, TBX20, and MEF2C.
source: These primordial cardiomyocytes expressed SMYD1 (SET and MYND domain-containing protein-1), a nuclear histone methyl-transferase involved in remodeling chromatin and sarcomere assembly (Li et al., 2011), Tbox transcription factors TBX5 and TBX20, two of the earliest markers of cardiac development (Bruneau et al., 2001; Takeuchi et al., 2005), and MEF2C, an essential transcription factor for sarcomere assembly and function (Lin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data with supporting citations for gene functions.

claim: From day eight onward, the expression of stem cell marker genes was extinguished while expression of cardiomyocyte differentiation transcripts increased.
source: From day eight onward, the expression of stem cell marker genes was extinguished while expression of cardiomyocyte differentiation transcripts increased (Figures 3C and 4C,D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figures 3C and 4C,D.

claim: Day 4 WT cells expressed hepatocyte nuclear factor family members (HNF1, HNF4A, HNF4B).
source: Day 4 WT cells expressed hepatocyte nuclear factor family members (HNF1, HNF4A, HNF4B) that are depleted in Gata6-null mice (Morrisey et al., 1998), FOXA1 and FOXA2, transcription factors that activate expression of the pancreas/duodenum homeobox-1 gene PDX1, which is essential for pancreas development and β islet cell differentiation (Gao et al., 2008; Gerrish et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2008) and other endodermal markers such as SOX17 (Wang et al., 2011; Figure 4A,B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A,B and Supplementary file 2, with supporting citations.

claim: FOXA1 and FOXA2 are transcription factors that activate expression of PDX1.
source: Day 4 WT cells expressed hepatocyte nuclear factor family members (HNF1, HNF4A, HNF4B) that are depleted in Gata6-null mice (Morrisey et al., 1998), FOXA1 and FOXA2, transcription factors that activate expression of the pancreas/duodenum homeobox-1 gene PDX1, which is essential for pancreas development and β islet cell differentiation (Gao et al., 2008; Gerrish et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2008) and other endodermal markers such as SOX17 (Wang et al., 2011; Figure 4A,B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2008; Gerrish et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2008.

claim: PDX1 is essential for pancreas development and β islet cell differentiation.
source: Day 4 WT cells expressed hepatocyte nuclear factor family members (HNF1, HNF4A, HNF4B) that are depleted in Gata6-null mice (Morrisey et al., 1998), FOXA1 and FOXA2, transcription factors that activate expression of the pancreas/duodenum homeobox-1 gene PDX1, which is essential for pancreas development and β islet cell differentiation (Gao et al., 2008; Gerrish et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2008) and other endodermal markers such as SOX17 (Wang et al., 2011; Figure 4A,B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2008; Gerrish et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2008.

claim: PDX1 was expressed through differentiation day 12 in WT lines, but not after metabolic enrichment for cardiomyocytes.
source: PDX1 was expressed through differentiation day 12 in WT lines, but not after metabolic enrichment for cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data across differentiation time points.

claim: GATA6+/- cells at day 4 had lower transcript levels of primordial cardiomyocyte genes compared to WT cells.
source: GATA6+/- cells at day 4 of differentiation had lower transcript levels of primordial cardiomyocyte genes compared to WT cells (Figure 3B,C) and gene ontology (GO) analyses inferred that pathways involved in cardiac muscle contraction, development, and chamber organization were reduced.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Gene ontology analyses inferred that pathways involved in cardiac muscle contraction, development, and chamber organization were reduced in GATA6+/- cells.
source: GATA6+/- cells at day 4 of differentiation had lower transcript levels of primordial cardiomyocyte genes compared to WT cells (Figure 3B,C) and gene ontology (GO) analyses inferred that pathways involved in cardiac muscle contraction, development, and chamber organization were reduced.
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of SMYD1 was strikingly diminished in GATA6+/- cells.
source: Notably, the expression of SMYD1, which regulates the expression of HAND2, a critical transcriptional regulator of the second heart field (Gottlieb et al., 2002; Laurent et al., 2017) that gives rise to the outflow tract, was strikingly diminished (Figure 3B–D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B-D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: SMYD1 regulates the expression of HAND2.
source: Notably, the expression of SMYD1, which regulates the expression of HAND2, a critical transcriptional regulator of the second heart field (Gottlieb et al., 2002; Laurent et al., 2017) that gives rise to the outflow tract, was strikingly diminished (Figure 3B–D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gottlieb et al., 2002; Laurent et al., 2017.

claim: HAND2 is a critical transcriptional regulator of the second heart field that gives rise to the outflow tract.
source: Notably, the expression of SMYD1, which regulates the expression of HAND2, a critical transcriptional regulator of the second heart field (Gottlieb et al., 2002; Laurent et al., 2017) that gives rise to the outflow tract, was strikingly diminished (Figure 3B–D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gottlieb et al., 2002; Laurent et al., 2017.

claim: Expression of multiple HAND2 network genes was lower in GATA6+/- cells than in WT cells.
source: Similarly, expression of multiple HAND2 network genes was also lower than in WT cells (Figure 3C,D), including GATA gene family members, ISL1, MEF2C, and prototypic cardiac transcription factors MEIS-1, NKX2-5, TBX5, and TBX20.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Forty of 54 PCGC patients with damaging variants in 11 HAND2-network and second heart field genes had outflow tract malformations.
source: Prompted by the transcriptional signatures in GATA6+/- cells, we compared the heart malformations in 54 PCGC patients with damaging variants in 11 HAND2-network and second heart field genes (Supplementary file 1C) with patients who have GATA6 mutations. Forty of these 54 patients also had outflow tract malformations, including all (n = 5) CHD patients with damaging de novo variants in TBX20.
evidence: This is based on clinical data from PCGC patients.

claim: All (n = 5) CHD patients with damaging de novo variants in TBX20 had outflow tract malformations.
source: Prompted by the transcriptional signatures in GATA6+/- cells, we compared the heart malformations in 54 PCGC patients with damaging variants in 11 HAND2-network and second heart field genes (Supplementary file 1C) with patients who have GATA6 mutations. Forty of these 54 patients also had outflow tract malformations, including all (n = 5) CHD patients with damaging de novo variants in TBX20.
evidence: This is based on clinical data from PCGC patients.

claim: The transient peak expression in WT cells of HOXA1, HOXB1, and MSX1 remained low throughout differentiation of GATA6+/- cells.
source: GATA6+/- cells also identified dysregulation of other gene programs involved in forming the outflow tract. The transient peak expression in WT cells of HOXA1, HOXB1, and MSX1, which regulate the induction and expression of critical molecules involved in specifying neural crest cell development (Makki and Capecchi, 2011; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Tvrdik and Capecchi, 2006), remained low throughout differentiation of GATA6+/- cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data with supporting citations for gene functions.

claim: HOXA1, HOXB1, and MSX1 regulate the induction and expression of critical molecules involved in specifying neural crest cell development.
source: GATA6+/- cells also identified dysregulation of other gene programs involved in forming the outflow tract. The transient peak expression in WT cells of HOXA1, HOXB1, and MSX1, which regulate the induction and expression of critical molecules involved in specifying neural crest cell development (Makki and Capecchi, 2011; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Tvrdik and Capecchi, 2006), remained low throughout differentiation of GATA6+/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makki and Capecchi, 2011; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Tvrdik and Capecchi, 2006.
